summary: Overall the proposed feature hypotheses are biologically and clinically plausible and align reasonably well with established stroke reperfusion knowledge. 'Onset-to-treatment time' is the strongest, highest-confidence modifier. Imaging-defined infarct core and age are also important but the submitted relative ranking (NIHSS above imaging core) is a minor misalignment with some imaging-centered literature. Validation suggestions are generally appropriate; main cross-cutting concerns are measurement error (onset time, ASPECTS), limited power for interaction tests in single trials, and potential confounding by selection/imaging criteria.

per_mechanism_scores.comments: Direct mechanistic link (penumbra salvage) is well-established; Emberson et al. and many meta-analyses support steep time-dependent benefit.
Older clots may be less amenable to fibrinolysis; plausible and supported by mechanistic and some clinical data, though less directly quantified than penumbra viability.
Time correlates with other system and stroke factors; this is a credible partial-explanation for observed interactions and is testable with mediation/adjustment.

strengths: Strong, specific mechanistic rationale linking earlier treatment to tissue salvage and better outcomes.
Well-supported by large pooled meta-analyses (Emberson et al. Lancet 2014 and others).
Validation recommendations (continuous interactions, splines, stratified bands) are appropriate and feasible.
weaknesses: Onset time measurement error (wake-up strokes) can bias interaction estimates and needs careful handling.
Some late presenters with favourable imaging can still benefit — simple time-only rules can over-simplify.
scored_features.justification: Time is the canonical and strongest effect modifier for IV alteplase; hypothesis is high priority for validation and is well-specified and testable.

per_mechanism_scores.comments: Age-related changes (collaterals, small vessel disease) plausibly reduce salvageable tissue; supported by subgroup analyses though effect on relative benefit is nuanced.
Increased hemorrhage risk with age is biologically plausible and observed; disentangling direct age effects from comorbidity is important.
Age is a proxy for frailty, pre-stroke disability and comorbidity; careful adjustment is necessary to avoid confounding.

strengths: Clinically intuitive and measurable feature with known associations to outcome and complications.
Validation suggestions (interaction tests, age bands, adjust for pre-stroke mRS) are appropriate.
weaknesses: Effect modification by age is complex: relative benefit often persists even when absolute benefit declines; statements must distinguish absolute vs relative effects.
Age may proxy unmeasured frailty; IST-3 included older patients which affects generalizability.
scored_features.justification: Age is a plausible and clinically important modifier. It warrants formal interaction testing with careful confounder adjustment, but it is less novel and requires nuance (absolute vs relative benefit).

per_mechanism_scores.comments: NIHSS reflects extent/territory of ischemia; mechanistic link to salvageable tissue exists but NIHSS is an imperfect surrogate for core/penumbra.
High severity relates to greater reperfusion injury risk, but this varies by cause (LVO vs small vessel) and collateral status.
NIHSS is strongly prognostic; interaction tests must separate prognostic from predictive effects (absolute vs relative differences).

strengths: NIHSS is routinely collected and clinically interpretable; analyses by NIHSS bands are feasible.
Mechanisms linking severity to both potential benefit (more to salvage) and harm (bigger core, hemorrhage) are described.
weaknesses: NIHSS is heterogeneous (e.g., a high score from cortical vs brainstem deficits has different implications) and does not directly measure core/penumbra.
The hypothesis states bidirectional effects which are plausible but make subgroup rules less straightforward and harder to operationalize.
scored_features.justification: NIHSS is important and testable, but its predictive value is mediated by imaging and stroke mechanism; expect heterogeneity and need to compare absolute vs relative effects.

scored_features.feature_name: Extent of early ischemic change / infarct core on baseline CT (ASPECTS / visible hypoattenuation)

per_mechanism_scores.comments: Large core means irreversible injury and broken microvasculature; biological rationale for reduced benefit and increased hemorrhage risk is strong and well-supported.
Alteplase may exacerbate blood-brain barrier disruption in large cores; plausible mechanistic route to increased sICH.
Core size correlates with time and severity; disentangling independent imaging effect requires adjustment and, ideally, perfusion data.

strengths: Strong biological and clinical rationale; imaging core is directly relevant to the mechanism of reperfusion benefit/harm.
Validation suggestions (ASPECTS interaction, CT perfusion when available, sICH mediation) are appropriate.
weaknesses: Relative ranking (ASPECTS as #4 below NIHSS) is arguably inconsistent with many imaging-focused analyses that treat core as a top modifier — this reduces evidence_alignment score.
ASPECTS on non-contrast CT has inter-rater variability and limited sensitivity, especially in IST-3-era imaging; measurement error can bias interaction estimates.
scored_features.justification: Imaging-defined core is mechanistically central and actionable, but practical measurement issues and the submitted lower ranking relative to NIHSS slightly reduce confidence; pursue validation, ideally with perfusion data or central imaging read.

per_mechanism_scores.comments: Hyperglycemia exacerbates ischemic injury and BBB breakdown — plausible mechanism though clinical effect-modification evidence is moderate.
Microvascular dysfunction and no-reflow are credible pathways to reduce benefit; evidence from observational studies but intervention trials for glucose control are inconclusive.
Acute hyperglycemia may reflect stroke severity/stress response rather than causal modifier; confounding is a real concern.

strengths: Biologically plausible and clinically measurable; HbA1c vs admission glucose distinction is recognized and validation plan addresses it.
Testable via interaction analyses and sICH comparisons.
weaknesses: Interventional data on glucose lowering in acute stroke do not clearly support modification of treatment effect, so causal impact is uncertain.
Acute glucose is confounded by stroke severity and stress responses; robust adjustment or instrumental strategies are needed.
scored_features.justification: Hyperglycemia is a plausible modifier worth exploring, particularly separating chronic diabetes (HbA1c) from acute stress hyperglycemia. Evidence for strong effect modification is moderate and confounding is an important limitation.

top_features: Extent of early ischemic change / infarct core on baseline CT (ASPECTS / visible hypoattenuation)
methodological_concerns: Onset-to-treatment time can be misclassified (uncertain or wake-up strokes); excluding or misclassifying these patients biases interaction estimates.

Imaging measures (ASPECTS, visible hypoattenuation) have inter-rater variability and limited sensitivity on non-contrast CT; IST-3-era scans may lack perfusion data, reducing ability to distinguish core vs penumbra.
Single-trial datasets often lack power to detect treatment �x feature interactions; meta-analytic pooling or prespecified pooled analyses are preferable.
Potential confounding by indication and unmeasured frailty (age, comorbidity, pre-stroke mRS) can create spurious interactions unless carefully adjusted.
Multiplicity: testing many interactions increases false-positive risk; prioritize pre-specified hypotheses and report effect sizes with CIs rather than relying solely on p-values.

Availability of the purported features in the provided dataset is unclear (available_features was empty); feasibility of proposed validations depends on actual data availability (NIHSS, ASPECTS, admission glucose, HbA1c).
